elements.id-string-352: This paper investigates the performance of the Generalized Covariance estimator ($GCov$) in estimating and identifying mixed causal and noncausal models.

elements.id-string-362: In recent years, there has been a growing interest in employing mixed causal and noncausal processes for the analysis of economic and financial time series (\cite{lanne2013noncausal}, \cite{hecq2016identification}, \cite{gourieroux2022nonlinear}, \cite{gourieroux2022nonlinear}, \cite{rygh2022causal}, and \cite{cavaliere2020bootstrapping}).
elements.id-string-363: These models have gained popularity due to their ability to incorporate both causal and noncausal components, enabling them to accurately capture the intricate nonlinear dynamics feature of economic and financial phenomena.
elements.id-string-364: In economics, the integration of both causal and noncausal components is particularly valuable when it comes to modeling expectations.
elements.id-string-365: Unlike the traditional autoregressive models, the mixed models offer insights into how economic variables are influenced by the expectations and mechanisms underlying the formation of these expectations (see \cite{lanne2011noncausal}, \cite{lanne2013noncausal}).
elements.id-string-366: In the financial domain, these models excel in capturing crucial phenomena characterized by nonlinear dynamics, including local trends, commonly referred to as speculative bubbles.
elements.id-string-367: Speculative bubbles are explosive financial patterns that frequently emerge in highly volatile markets, like the cryptocurrency and commodity markets.
elements.id-string-368: These bubbles represent periods of excessive prices (rates), driven more by market psychology and speculation than underlying fundamentals.
elements.id-string-369: During such episodes, asset prices surge to unsustainable levels, often followed by a sudden and sharp decline, leading to adverse economic outcomes.
elements.id-string-370: Hence, the identification and analysis of these speculative bubbles are of crucial importance due to their potential to disrupt economic stability and resource allocation (see \cite{gourieroux2017noncausal}, \cite{fries2019mixed}, and \cite{hecq2021forecasting}).
elements.id-string-371: \indent The estimation techniques available for mixed causal and noncausal processes fall into two main categories: parametric and semi-parametric estimators.
elements.id-string-372: Parametric methods, such as the Maximum Likelihood estimator (\cite{lanne2013noncausal} and \cite{davis2020noncausal}), yield efficient estimates when the error distribution is correctly specified but become inefficient or even inconsistent when this assumption is violated.
elements.id-string-373: In contrast, semi-parametric methods offer the advantage of robustness to specification errors and do not require distributional assumption on the errors of the model (\cite{gourieroux2017noncausal}, \cite{gourieroux2022generalized}, and \cite{hecq2022spectral}).
elements.id-string-374: As a consequence, the benefit of employing a semi-parametric estimator is evident.
elements.id-string-375: Currently, the only time domain semi-parametric estimator available for estimating mixed causal and noncausal models is the Generalized Covariance estimator ($GCov$).
elements.id-string-376: It was initially introduced by \cite{gourieroux2017noncausal} in the context of noncausal models and subsequently extended to a semi-parametrically efficient estimator in \cite{gourieroux2022generalized}.
elements.id-string-377: The $GCov$ is characterized by an objective function based on the autocovariances of linear and nonlinear functions of independent and identically distributed ($i.i.d.$) errors.
elements.id-string-378: \indent To address the issues related to local minima and avoid the misestimation of our processes, we propose combining the $GCov$ estimator with the Simulated Annealing (SA) optimization algorithm.
elements.id-string-379: SA is a powerful metaheuristic method designed specifically to capture the global minimum when the objective function contains numerous local minima.
elements.id-string-380: Initially proposed by \cite{kirkpatrick1983optimization}, SA draws inspiration from the annealing process of solids to tackle optimization problems.
elements.id-string-381: Over the years, SA has demonstrated remarkable success in solving complex optimization problems in various fields, including computer (VLSI) design, image processing, molecular physics, and chemistry (see, for instance, \cite{wong2012simulated}, \cite{carnevali1987image}, \cite{jones1991molecular}, and \cite{pannetier1990prediction}).
elements.id-string-382: By integrating SA with the $GCov$ estimator, this paper presents a significant improvement in the performance of the $GCov$ estimator applied to the mixed causal and noncausal models.
elements.id-string-383: \indent It is important to note that this paper exclusively focuses on the estimation of causal and noncausal parameters.
elements.id-string-384: We do not consider inference on estimated parameters neither the significance of $GCov$ Portmanteau type tests (see \cite{gourieroux2022generalized}, and \cite{jasiakneyazi}, respectively).
elements.id-string-385: Indeed these latter important points are dependent on the correct identification and specification of those models.
elements.id-string-386: Also, this paper primarily studies the application of the $GCov$ estimator for multivariate models.
elements.id-string-387: We also present some results for univariate processes with the purpose of illustrating the graphical behavior of the objective function estimator when expressed as a function of a single parameter.
elements.id-string-388: In this context, alternative strategies may be employed to achieve a successful convergence of $GCov$.
elements.id-string-389: For example, a grid search strategy over the initial values to then select the estimation that yields a lower objective function value (see \cite{bec2020mixed} for a grid search approach when applied to the parametric framework).
elements.id-string-390: However, applying this alternative methodology in the multivariate framework can be challenging due to the large dimensions of the grid arrangement.

elements.id-string-593: It is worth noting that, in our approach, the final temperature $T^{o}_{MIN}$ is a deterministic function of $T^{o}_{MAX}$, $r$, and $Q$.
elements.id-string-594: This is true because $T^{o}_{MIN}$ is obtained through $Q$ reductions at a rate of $r$ from the initial value $T^{o}_{MAX}$, i.e., $T^{o}_{MIN} = T^{o}_{MIN}(T^{o}_{MAX}, r, Q)$.
elements.id-string-595: \indent In the literature, it is common to employ a cooling rate of $r=0.85$, as indicated in \cite{goffe1994global} and \cite{corana1987minimizing}.
elements.id-string-596: However, determining suitable values for $T^{o}_{MAX}$ and $Q$, which subsequently determine $T^{o}_{MIN}$, often requires an empirical approach.
elements.id-string-597: Therefore, before conducting our MC experiment, we undertake a preliminary analysis of the behavior of the $DGP$ under investigation by initially setting $T^{o}_{MAX}$ and $Q$ to high values.
elements.id-string-598: This allows us to monitor the performance of the objective function throughout the optimization process.
elements.id-string-599: More specifically, in this preliminary analysis, we set $T^{o}_{MAX}=5000$ and $Q=150$.
elements.id-string-600: Figure 5-(a) illustrates the behavior of the objective function of $GCov22$ as a function of the number of iterations $Q$.
elements.id-string-601: The objective value of $GCov22$, from the first approximately 50 iterations, fluctuates around an average value of 2.7 without leading to any improvements for our optimization problem.
elements.id-string-602: This suggests that $T^{o}_{MAX}=5000$ is excessively high and results in inefficient use of time.
elements.id-string-603: Around $Q=50$, corresponding to $T^{o}=1.5$, the objective function decreases and converges toward the global optimum.
elements.id-string-604: These results are further confirmed by Figure 5-(b), which depicts the behavior of the parameter $\theta$ as a function of $Q$.
elements.id-string-605: Based on the insights gained from this analysis, we set $T_{MAX}=1.5$ and $Q=100$ in our MC experiment.
elements.id-string-606: Furthermore, to effectively explore the search space we set $M=100$.
elements.id-string-607: The choice of a high value for $M$ is crucial for a comprehensive exploration of the search space.
elements.id-string-608: The results are presented in Figure 5-(c) and summarized in Table 1.
elements.id-string-609: Now, the SA algorithm yields a significant improvement in results compared to Section 3.1: $\hat{\theta}$ closely approximates the true value, and the true dynamic is captured $90\%$ of the time.

elements.id-string-635: \indent Having identified $p=2$ as the appropriate order, we apply the $GCov22$ method to the demeaned data and reject the null hypothesis of the Gaussianity of the residuals.
elements.id-string-636: In this specific case, we use both the OLS estimate ($\Theta_{OLS}$) and the results obtained by the SA method as starting points for the BFGS optimization problems.
elements.id-string-637: The results are presented in Table 2.
elements.id-string-638: Notably, Table 2 highlights that the choice of the initial guess significantly affects the results.
elements.id-string-639: When we employ the OLS strategy to determine the initial guess, the $GCov22$ method identifies the process as purely causal VAR($2$).
elements.id-string-640: However, when we utilize the SA method, we obtain a lower value of the $GCov22$ objective function, and the bivariate process is identified as a mixed causal and noncausal VAR($2$) with three roots outside the unit circle and one root inside the unit circle.
elements.id-string-641: Indeed, the eigenvalues in the latter case lie both inside and outside the unit circle: $j_1=0.972$, $j_2=0.88$, $j_3=0.604$, and $j_4=-4.355$.
elements.id-string-642: These findings underscore the importance of combining SA with $GCov22$.
elements.id-string-643: Employing SA to capture the initial guess is crucial in this case, enabling us to identify a non-causal component of the process, which, in turn, allows us to capture the nonlinear features that define these series.
